summary: Presents further design concepts for datalanguage, the language of CCA's datacomputer project. It gives preliminary results of the language design, a model for the semantics of data language, and notes on future considerations.

eli5.summary: People were designing a language for asking a big data-storage computer for information. This paper shares their ideas so far.

questions: how to share data across different computers
subtitle: Language design for a network data utility system

tldr.problem: As computer networks grew, researchers wanted to build a specialized data management utility that could serve many different computers with diverse hardware and programming languages, but there was no suitable language for requesting services from such a system.
tldr.mechanism: The datacomputer project at CCA designed a dedicated data management system paired with a specialized language (datalanguage) that allowed any networked computer to request data operations in a hardware-independent way, with support for different views of the same data.
tldr.outcome: This work established foundational concepts in distributed data management and query language design that influenced later work in networked database systems and data sharing protocols.

today: RFC 610 documents early thinking about distributed data management and query languages for network-based systems. While datalanguage itself did not achieve widespread adoption, the conceptual work influenced later database systems and network data services. The problems it identified—data independence, multiple views, efficient selection, and format translation—remain central to database and data integration work.

sections.title: The Datacomputer and Its Purpose
sections.content:
The datacomputer was a new kind of network service: a specialized computer dedicated entirely to data management and storage. Unlike general-purpose computers, the datacomputer was designed to manage vast databases—files storing hundreds of billions of bits—and serve them efficiently to computers across the ARPANET.

The vision was bold: support data sharing among processes running on radically different hardware, under different operating systems, written in different programming languages. All of them would need to access the same shared databases. The datacomputer would handle the translation between each computer's native formats and the shared data, so users did not need to worry about whether data was stored on special magnetic tape, disk drives, or mass storage systems.

Datalanguage was the only way to communicate with the datacomputer: it was the exclusive interface for data description, creation, retrieval, modification, and access to services. Every operation the datacomputer could perform had to be expressible in datalanguage.
sections.eli5: The datacomputer was a very big library on the network that many different computers could ask for information. Datalanguage was the language everyone had to use to ask the library questions, no matter what kind of computer they were using.

sections.title: The Challenge of Data Sharing
sections.content:
The RFC identifies a central problem in distributed data management: different users of the same database may need completely different views of the data.

For example, consider a university database with information about students, teachers, and subjects. One application program might want to see data organized as (student, teacher, subject) triples. Another might want it organized by student first, with all of that student's teachers and subjects nested underneath. A third might want it organized by teacher. All three views are legitimate, but none of them matches how the data is physically stored.

The datacomputer had to support multiple modes: some applications wanted complete independence from storage details and would let the system optimize access. Others needed direct control over access strategies for efficiency. The language had to accommodate all of these requirements without forcing each application programmer to understand the internals of data storage and organization.
sections.eli5: The tricky part was that different programs wanted to see the same information in different ways, like sorting the same pile of photos by date or by person. The language had to let each program see the data its own way, without making them all learn how the data was really stored.

sections.title: Design for a Network
sections.content:
The datacomputer was designed to be just one node in the ARPANET (which had over 60 nodes at the time). This imposed special requirements on the language design.

Because network bandwidth was limited (typical transfer rates were only 30 kilobits per second—millions of times slower than today), the language had to support efficient data selection. Rather than transferring entire files, applications needed to specify exactly which parts of a database they wanted, so only that data would cross the network.

The language also had to enable multiple processes running on different network nodes to cooperate on a single task. For example, one process might run on the ILLIAC IV supercomputer for array manipulation, another on the datacomputer for data retrieval, another on MULTICS for general programming, and another on a TIP for user interaction. All four would need to share data through the datacomputer's common language.
sections.eli5: Since the network was slow, the language had to let you ask for just the data you needed, not everything. Also, different computers on the network had to be able to work together by talking to the same library.
